subject: maths
title: Chapter 9 · Test 4
summary: A 15-question test on Year 9 Chapter 9: histograms and stem-and-leaf plots, shape of distributions, centre and spread, two-step chance experiments and tree diagrams.
body:
This test covers Chapter 9, Probability and statistics: histograms and stem-and-leaf plots, the shape of data distributions, measures of centre and spread, two-step chance experiments and tree diagrams.

## How to do this test

- **Time:** about 25 minutes.
- **Conditions:** no notes and no calculator unless the question says. Show your working on paper.
- **Diagrams:** many questions have a histogram, table of outcomes or tree diagram — read the numbers on it carefully.
- **Levels:** 4 easy, 5 medium, 4 hard and 2 challenge questions.
- **After marking:** for each question you got wrong, go back to the lesson it came from and redo its worked examples. Then try another Chapter 9 test — each one has different questions on the same skills.

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the daily maximum temperatures (°C) in a town over 31 days. How many days were in the class 14 to less than 18 °C?
questions.explanation: The bar from 14 to 18 reaches a height of 5. The neighbouring bar (9) is for the next class.
steps: Find the bar that starts at 14 and ends at 18.
Read its height on the frequency axis: 5.

mistakes.A: Step 1: that is the bar for 18 to less than 22. Find the bar that starts at 14.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 14 is a class boundary on the horizontal axis. Read the bar’s height on the frequency axis.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 29 adds every bar from 14 upwards. Read just the one bar from 14 to 18.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of the daily maximum temperatures (°C) in a town over 31 days, with class boundaries 10, 14, 18, 22, 26, 30, 34 and frequencies 2, 5, 9, 8, 5, 2

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the ages of 70 people at a family picnic. Which word best describes the shape of the distribution?
questions.explanation: It is bimodal: it has two clear peaks with a dip between them. Look at the whole display, not just one bar.
steps: Look for the peak (or peaks) and for any long tail.
Here it has two clear peaks with a dip between them, so it is bimodal.

mistakes.B: Step 1: there are two separate peaks with a dip between them. Count the peaks first.
mistakes.C: Step 1: there are two separate peaks with a dip between them. Count the peaks first.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the halves may look alike, but the key feature is the two separate peaks. Count the peaks first.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of the ages of 70 people at a family picnic, with class boundaries 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70 and frequencies 16, 10, 3, 6, 15, 12, 8

questions.prompt: The heights (cm) of 7 seedlings: 41, 35, 50, 44, 38, 29, 36. What is the median?
questions.explanation: In order: 29, 35, 36, 38, 41, 44, 50. The middle (4th) value is 38. Taking the middle of the unordered list gives 44, which is wrong.
steps: 7 values, so the median is the 4th: 38.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 44 is the middle of the list as written. Put the values in order first.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 39 is the mean (total ÷ 7). The median is the middle value of the ordered list.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 21 is the range (50 − 29). The median is the middle value.

questions.prompt: A spinner with 3 equal coloured sections is spun and a six-sided die is rolled. How many different outcomes are there?
questions.explanation: Every one of the 3 outcomes of the first step can pair with every one of the 6 outcomes of the second: 3 × 6 = 18. Adding (9) misses most of the pairs.
steps: Step 1 has 3 outcomes and step 2 has 6.

mistakes.A: Step 2: you added 3 + 6. Each of the 3 first results pairs with each of the 6 second results, so multiply.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 6 counts only the die. Each die result can come with any of the 3 colours.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 6 × 6 is for two dice. The spinner has only 3 outcomes.

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the distances (m) 40 students threw a ball. How many were 25 m or more?
questions.explanation: The bars from 25 upwards have heights 10 + 6 + 2 = 18. Using only the first of those bars (10) misses the rest.
steps: "25 or more" means every bar that starts at 25 or higher.

mistakes.B: Step 1: 10 is only the bar from 25 to 30. Every bar further right is also "25 or more".
mistakes.C: Step 1: you included the bar from 20 to 25. Start at the bar that begins at 25.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 22 counts the values LESS than 25. Add the bars from 25 upwards.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of the distances (m) 40 students threw a ball, with class boundaries 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40 and frequencies 3, 7, 12, 10, 6, 2

questions.prompt: The number of pages 8 students read: 6, 14, 10, 5, 3, 19, 12, 18. Find the interquartile range.
questions.explanation: Ordered: 3, 5, 6, 10, 12, 14, 18, 19. Q1 = (5 + 6) ÷ 2 = 5.5 and Q3 = (14 + 18) ÷ 2 = 16, so IQR = 10.5. The range (16) uses the extremes instead.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 16 is the range (19 − 3). The IQR is Q3 − Q1.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 11 is the median of the whole set. The IQR is the difference between the quartiles.
mistakes.D: Step 2: each half has 4 values, so its median is the AVERAGE of its two middle values, not one of them.

questions.prompt: Two spinners each have three equal sections numbered 1, 2 and 3. Both are spun and the numbers are added (see the table). What is the probability that the sum is 4?
questions.explanation: Three of the 9 cells show 4 — (1, 3), (2, 2), (3, 1) — so P = 3/9 = 1/3. 1/5 wrongly treats the five sums as equally likely.

mistakes.B: Step 1: the 5 possible sums (2 to 6) are not equally likely. Count the 9 equally likely cells.
mistakes.C: Step 2: (2, 2) also gives 4. Count every cell showing 4.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 4 can be made in more than one way: (1, 3), (2, 2) and (3, 1).

questions.diagram_alt: A 3 by 3 table of sums of two spinners numbered 1 to 3: the cells show 2, 3, 4 / 3, 4, 5 / 4, 5, 6

questions.prompt: Ari scores a free throw with probability 0.8, so he misses with probability 0.2, independently each time. He takes two shots. Use the tree diagram to find the probability that he misses both.
questions.explanation: Missing both means miss AND miss: 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.04. Adding gives 0.4, which would make two misses more likely than one.
steps: Follow the path Miss then Miss.

mistakes.A: Step 2: along a path you multiply, not add: 0.2 × 0.2.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 0.2 is only the first shot. Both shots must be misses.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 0.2 × 0.8 is miss then SCORE. Follow the miss–miss path.

questions.diagram_alt: A tree diagram with Miss 0.2 and Score 0.8 for the first shot, and Miss 0.2 and Score 0.8 again after each

questions.prompt: A data set has a mean of 61 and a median of 68. Which shape is it most likely to have?
questions.explanation: The mean (61) is less than the median (68), so some small values are dragging the mean down — a tail to the left, negatively skewed.
steps: The mean is pulled towards the long tail; the median hardly moves.
Mean (61) less than median (68) → tail towards small values → negatively skewed.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the mean is pulled towards the tail. Mean BELOW median means the tail points to the smaller values: negative.
mistakes.B: Step 1: in a symmetric distribution the mean and median are about equal. These differ by 7.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the mean and median can’t show two peaks. Their difference points to a skew.

questions.prompt: The histogram shows how far (km) 80 people travel to work. What percentage of them were less than 10 km from work?
questions.explanation: 10 + 22 = 32 out of 80, and 32 ÷ 80 × 100 = 40%. Giving 32% forgets to divide by the total.
steps: Bars that are less than 10 km from work: 10 + 22 = 32.

mistakes.A: Step 1: you used only one bar (22). Include every bar that is less than 10 km from work.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 32 is the NUMBER of them. Divide by the total of 80 and multiply by 100.
mistakes.C: Step 1: you included one bar too many. Check where "less than 10 km from work" starts and stops on the horizontal axis.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of how far (km) 80 people travel to work, with class boundaries 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 and frequencies 10, 22, 20, 12, 8, 6, 2

questions.prompt: 8 bowling scores have a mean of 15. 7 of them are 12, 18, 9, 20, 14, 16, 9. What is the last one?
questions.explanation: All 8 must total 15 × 8 = 120; the known ones total 98, so the last is 120 − 98 = 22. Guessing it equals the mean is the common slip.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the missing value does not have to equal the mean. Use total = mean × number of values.
mistakes.C: Step 1: there are 8 values, so the total is 15 × 8, not 15 × 7.
mistakes.D: Step 1: that is the mean of the 7 known values. Find the total needed for all 8.

questions.prompt: A drawer has 3 black and 4 grey socks. Two socks are taken without replacement. Use the tree diagram to find the probability that they are the same colour.
questions.explanation: Black–black = 3/7 × 2/6 = 6/42 and grey–grey = 4/7 × 3/6 = 12/42, so P(same) = 18/42 = 3/7. Using only grey–grey gives 2/7.

mistakes.A: Step 2: (3/7)² + (4/7)² is WITH replacement. Use the tree’s second-stage fractions out of 6.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 2/7 is only grey–grey. Black–black is also the same colour — add both paths.
mistakes.D: Step 3: 4/7 is the chance of DIFFERENT colours. Use the black–black and grey–grey paths.

questions.diagram_alt: A tree diagram for two socks without replacement (Bk = black, Gy = grey): first Bk 3/7 and Gy 4/7; after Bk, Bk 2/6 and Gy 4/6; after Gy, Bk 3/6 and Gy 3/6

questions.prompt: A coin is tossed and a die is rolled. What is the probability of getting a head OR a 6 (or both)?
questions.explanation: The 12-cell table has 6 cells with a head plus (T, 6): 7 cells, so P = 7/12. Adding 1/2 + 1/6 = 2/3 counts (H, 6) twice.
steps: Head: H1 to H6 (6 cells). A 6 without a head: T6 (1 more cell). Total 7.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 1/2 + 1/6 counts (H, 6) twice. Count the cells in a 2 × 6 table instead.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 1/12 is a head AND a 6. "Or" includes every head and every 6.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 1/2 counts only the heads. (T, 6) also has a 6.

questions.prompt: Class A has 20 students with a mean test mark of 70. Class B has 30 students with a mean of 80. What is the mean mark of all 50 students together?
questions.explanation: Total marks = 20 × 70 + 30 × 80 = 1400 + 2400 = 3800, and 3800 ÷ 50 = 76. Simply averaging 70 and 80 (75) ignores the bigger class.
steps: Class A total = 20 × 70 = 1400. Class B total = 30 × 80 = 2400.

mistakes.B: Step 2: averaging the two means ignores that Class B has more students. Use the totals.
mistakes.C: Step 1: you multiplied each class size by the OTHER class’s mean. Class A total = 20 × 70.
mistakes.D: Step 2: adding the means does not give a mean. Divide the combined total by 50.

questions.prompt: A bag has 4 red counters and 1 blue counter. You win a prize if the blue counter is one of the two you take out (without replacement). What is the probability of winning?
questions.explanation: P(no blue) = 4/5 × 3/4 = 3/5, so P(win) = 1 − 3/5 = 2/5. (Check: blue first 1/5 + red then blue 4/5 × 1/4 = 1/5, total 2/5.)

mistakes.A: Step 2: 4/5 × 3/4 = 3/5 is the chance of NOT getting blue. Subtract it from 1.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 1 − (4/5)² is WITH replacement. Without replacement the second pick is out of 4.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 1/5 is the chance of blue on the FIRST pick only. Blue could also come second.
